claim: Diphenylcyclopropenone (DPC) is an organic chemical hapten which induces allergic contact dermatitis.
source: Diphenylcyclopropenone (DPC) is an organic chemical hapten which induces allergic contact dermatitis and is used in the treatment of warts, melanoma, and alopecia areata.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of DPC.

claim: DPC is used in the treatment of warts, melanoma, and alopecia areata.
source: Diphenylcyclopropenone (DPC) is an organic chemical hapten which induces allergic contact dermatitis and is used in the treatment of warts, melanoma, and alopecia areata.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Repeated exposure to DPC induced highly dynamic transient expansions of a polyclonal diverse T cell population.
source: Repeated exposure to DPC induced highly dynamic transient expansions of a polyclonal diverse T cell population.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The number of TCRs expanded early after sensitization varies between individuals and predicts the magnitude of the allergic reaction.
source: The number of TCRs expanded early after sensitization varies between individuals and predicts the magnitude of the allergic reaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The expanded TCRs show preferential TCR V and J gene usage.
source: The expanded TCRs show preferential TCR V and J gene usage and consist of clusters of TCRs with similar sequences, two characteristic features of antigen-driven responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The expanded TCRs consist of clusters of TCRs with similar sequences.
source: The expanded TCRs show preferential TCR V and J gene usage and consist of clusters of TCRs with similar sequences, two characteristic features of antigen-driven responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Preferential V and J gene usage and TCR clustering are characteristic features of antigen-driven responses.
source: The expanded TCRs show preferential TCR V and J gene usage and consist of clusters of TCRs with similar sequences, two characteristic features of antigen-driven responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations in the discussion.

claim: The expanded TCRs share subtle sequence motifs that can be captured using a dynamic Bayesian network.
source: The expanded TCRs share subtle sequence motifs that can be captured using a dynamic Bayesian network.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the DBN analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The response to DPC is mediated by a polyclonal population of T cells recognizing a small number of dominant antigens.
source: These observations suggest the response to DPC is mediated by a polyclonal population of T cells recognizing a small number of dominant antigens.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the observed TCR expansion patterns, V/J gene usage, and clustering.

claim: DPC is a potent skin sensitizer.
source: It is a potent skin sensitizer (Mose et al., 2017a; Stute et al., 1981) and, since it is non-mutagenic in the AMES assay (Wilkerson et al., 1987), it has been used as an immunostimulant in the treatment of warts (Buckley et al., 1999), melanoma (Read et al., 2017), and alopecia (Ashworth et al., 1989; Karanovic et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DPC is non-mutagenic in the AMES assay.
source: It is a potent skin sensitizer (Mose et al., 2017a; Stute et al., 1981) and, since it is non-mutagenic in the AMES assay (Wilkerson et al., 1987), it has been used as an immunostimulant in the treatment of warts (Buckley et al., 1999), melanoma (Read et al., 2017), and alopecia (Ashworth et al., 1989; Karanovic et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Wilkerson et al., 1987.

claim: DPC can act as an adjuvant to conventional immunization.
source: DPC can also act as an adjuvant to conventional immunization (von Moos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to von Moos et al., 2012.

claim: DPC is not commonly found in the environment.
source: Because of its clinical applications, and because it is not commonly found in the environment, DPC serves as an interesting model to study primary and secondary responses to chemical haptens in humans, although the confounding effects of any underlying clinical condition in the treated individuals must obviously be considered.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for using DPC as a model system.

claim: The magnitude of allergic contact dermatitis to DPC does not continue to increase during repeated exposure.
source: Clinically, repeated exposure results in rapid sensitization, but the magnitude of the resulting allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) does not continue to increase during repeated exposure (Mose et al., 2017a), suggesting the existence of regulatory processes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Mose et al., 2017a.

claim: The lack of continued increase in ACD magnitude during repeated DPC exposure suggests the existence of regulatory processes.
source: Clinically, repeated exposure results in rapid sensitization, but the magnitude of the resulting allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) does not continue to increase during repeated exposure (Mose et al., 2017a), suggesting the existence of regulatory processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the introduction based on the observed clinical pattern.

claim: Global expression profiling at the site of DPC elicitation suggested a predominantly Th1/Th17 type T cell infiltration.
source: Global expression profiling at the site of elicitation suggested a predominantly Th1/Th17 type T cell infiltration, whose dynamics mirrored the clinical and histopathological picture (Mose et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Mose et al., 2017b.

claim: The dynamics of Th1/Th17 T cell infiltration at the DPC elicitation site mirrored the clinical and histopathological picture.
source: Global expression profiling at the site of elicitation suggested a predominantly Th1/Th17 type T cell infiltration, whose dynamics mirrored the clinical and histopathological picture (Mose et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Mose et al., 2017b.

claim: High serum IL4 and low IL12 were observed in patients with alopecia showing a favorable response to DPC treatment.
source: High serum interleukin-4 (IL4) and low interleukin-12 (IL12) were observed in patients with alopecia showing a favorable response to DPC treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a previous observation, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: TCR sequencing was carried out on unfractionated blood samples from 29 patients with alopecia.
source: We carried out TCRseq on unfractionated blood samples from 29 patients with alopecia (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design in the Results section.

claim: Samples were collected before and at one to three time points after sensitization with DPC.
source: Samples were collected before (referred to as the pre-sensitization [PS] sample, week 0, n = 25 samples) and at one to three time points after sensitization with DPC (Figure 1A), taken at 2 weeks (PT1, n = 23), 6 weeks (PT2, n = 18), and approximately 24 weeks (PT3, n = 17) post-sensitization.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design in the Results section.

claim: TCR sequencing was performed on five healthy volunteers as controls.
source: As controls, we carried out TCRseq on five healthy volunteers, for which we had time points that matched the 0-, 2-, and 6-week time points of the DPC sensitized group.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design in the Results section.

claim: A total of 24,431,855 distinct TCR sequences were obtained, of which 17,451,853 were unique across all samples.
source: We obtained a total of 24,431,855 distinct TCR sequences, of which 17,451,853 were unique across all samples.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sequencing results in the Results section.

claim: The median number of TCRs per sample was 95,638 (range 23,224–690,600).
source: The median number of TCRs per sample was 95,638 (range 23,224–690,600) and the median number of unique TCRs per sample was 75,111 (range 19,095–342,336).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sequencing results in the Results section.

claim: The median number of unique TCRs per sample was 75,111 (range 19,095–342,336).
source: The median number of TCRs per sample was 95,638 (range 23,224–690,600) and the median number of unique TCRs per sample was 75,111 (range 19,095–342,336).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sequencing results in the Results section.

claim: The major T cell sub-populations did not change significantly after exposure to DPC.
source: The major T cell sub-populations (CD4/CD8, naive, central memory, effector memory, and effector memory RA revertant) (Fletcher et al., 2005) were quantified by flow cytometry and did not change significantly after exposure to DPC (Figure 1B, two-sided paired t-tests corrected for multiple testing, p=0.48, p=0.74, p=0.49, and p=0.74 for CD4, and Figure 1C, p=0.11, p=0.72, p=0.72, and p=0.37 for CD8 naive, central, effector, and effector memory RA revertant cells respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: TCR repertoire diversity did not differ significantly before and after exposure to DPC.
source: Similarly, TCR repertoire diversity, captured by the Shannon diversity index, or the clonal expansion captured by the Gini inequality coefficient, did not differ significantly before and after exposure to DPC (Figure 1D,E, Kruskal–Wallis rank sum tests, p=0.89 and p=0.90 respectively), nor between the different time points post-sensitization (Figure 1G,H, Kruskal–Wallis rank sum tests, p=0.96 and p=0.95 respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 1D, 1E, 1G, and 1H.

claim: The number of TCRs found at frequencies above 1 in 1000 did not change as a result of sensitization.
source: Finally, the number of TCRs found at frequencies above 1 in 1000, which correspond to the most abundant 6% of the repertoire on average, did not change as a result of sensitization (Figure 1F,I, Kruskal–Wallis rank sum tests, p=0.12 and p=0.91 respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 1F and 1I.

claim: There was no evidence that exposure to DPC caused global alterations in the structure of the TCR repertoire.
source: There was therefore no evidence that exposure to DPC, a potent skin sensitizer, caused global alterations in the structure of the TCR repertoire.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the analyses of diversity, clonality, and T cell subpopulations.

claim: In a number of individuals, there was a population of TCRs which were absent before sensitization and present at relatively high abundance after sensitization.
source: We observed that in a number of individuals, there was a population of TCRs which were absent before sensitization and present at relatively high abundance after sensitization (indicated by the pink dots in the left panels of Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The range of percentages of expanded TCRs at PT1 is much greater in the patients than in the healthy volunteers.
source: The range of percentages of expanded TCRs at PT1 is clearly much greater in the patients than in the healthy volunteers (between 0 and 2 weeks), although the medians are not significantly different (p=0.16 and p=0.47 for alpha and beta respectively, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The percentage of expanded TCRs at PT1 in the patients is significantly larger than the percentage of TCRs which were expanded at PS and absent at PT1.
source: The percentage of expanded TCRs at PT1 in the patients is significantly larger than the percentage of TCRs which were expanded at PS and absent at PT1 (p=0.02 for alpha, p=0.03 for beta, Wilcoxon signed–rank).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of PT1 expanded TCR alpha and TCR beta sequences was highly correlated.
source: The number of PT1 expanded TCR alpha and TCR beta sequences was highly correlated (Spearman's rho = 0.85, p<0.0001, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: After the initial increase post-sensitization, the number of expanded TCRs remained rather constant over the later time points.
source: After the initial increase post-sensitization, the number of expanded TCRs remained rather constant over the later time points.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on longitudinal analysis.

claim: There was no evidence that the total number of expanded TCRs increased with time despite repeated therapeutic stimulation with sensitizer.
source: There was no evidence that the total number of expanded TCRs increased with time, despite the fact that individuals were exposed to repeated therapeutic stimulation with sensitizer on a weekly basis for the period of the study in addition to the patch test applications (Figure 1A) (Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test, p=0.92 alpha and p=0.36 beta).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on statistical analysis of longitudinal data.

claim: The majority of PT1 (2 weeks) expanded TCRs decreased or returned to baseline at subsequent time points.
source: The majority of PT1 (2 weeks) expanded TCRs decreased or returned to baseline at subsequent time points (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of PT2 expanded TCRs present at 6 weeks were not expanded at 2 weeks, peaked at 6 weeks, and decreased or returned to baseline by around 24 weeks.
source: The majority of PT2 expanded TCRs present at 6 weeks were not expanded at 2 weeks, peaked at 6 weeks, and decreased or returned to baseline by the time the PT3 sample was taken at around 24 weeks (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Exposure to repeated doses of DPC induced large, but predominantly transient, changes in the frequencies of a small proportion of the TCRs.
source: The exposure to repeated doses of DPC therefore induced large, but predominantly transient, changes in the frequencies of a small proportion of the TCRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the longitudinal TCR dynamics data.

claim: Exposure to DPC induced skin sensitization in almost all individuals but the magnitude of the response varied significantly between individuals.
source: Exposure to DPC induced skin sensitization (patch test scores of + or higher) in almost all individuals but the magnitude of the response varied significantly between individuals (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The maximum skin response to DPC was usually observed at the first patch test, and declined or remained constant thereafter despite repeated exposure.
source: Interestingly, the maximum response was usually observed at the first patch test, and declined or remained constant thereafter despite repeated exposure (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: The number of PT1 expanded TCRs was positively correlated to the patch test score.
source: The number of PT1 expanded TCRs was positively correlated to the patch test score.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was no significant association between the number of PS expanded TCRs and the PT1 patch test score.
source: In contrast, there was no significant association between the number of PS expanded TCRs and the PT1 patch test score (Figure 4C, right panels).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: The numbers of expanded TCRs at PT1 were correlated with the strength of the reaction recorded at the sensitization site, and with the patch test score at PT1 (2 weeks), as well as PT2 (6 weeks).
source: As illustrated above, the numbers of expanded TCRs at PT1 were correlated with the strength of the reaction recorded at the sensitization site, and with the patch test score at PT1 (2 weeks), as well as PT2 (6 weeks).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: The correlation between expanded TCRs and patch test scores was lost at PT3 (24 weeks).
source: The correlation was lost at PT3 (24 weeks), perhaps reflecting the greatly decreased range of patch test scores at this time point (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section with a speculative explanation.

claim: Several V and J regions were skewed in several different individuals, suggesting some common driver of V/J gene usage.
source: Interestingly, some V and J regions were skewed in several different individuals, suggesting some common driver of V/J gene usage, despite the fact that the individuals were not related.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on the V/J gene usage analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The expanded TCRs formed significantly more large clusters of 'related' TCRs than control sets.
source: The expanded TCRs formed significantly more large clusters of 'related' TCRs than either control sets (Figure 6B,C (i)).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: The sequences in the largest cluster of CDR3 beta sequences showed a high level of similarity consistent with belonging to a set of TCRs with shared specificities.
source: The sequences showed a high level of similarity consistent with belonging to a set of TCRs with shared specificities (Dash et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on sequence alignment analysis and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The skewing of V and J genes, and the presence of clusters of similar TCRs were strongly suggestive that the expanded TCRs were enriched for TCRs responding to a limited number of specific epitopes.
source: Taken together, the skewing of V and J genes, and the presence of clusters of similar TCRs were strongly suggestive that the expanded TCRs were enriched for TCRs responding to a limited number of specific epitopes.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The DBN could classify the full DPC/control test sets with mean accuracy of 94%.
source: The DBN classifier could classify the full DPC/control test sets with mean accuracy of 94% from 10 repeats of 10-fold cross validation, and sets of 10 sequences with mean accuracy 77.7% (Figure 7C upper panel).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on the DBN classification analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The DBN could classify sets of 10 DPC/control sequences with mean accuracy 77.7%.
source: The DBN classifier could classify the full DPC/control test sets with mean accuracy of 94% from 10 repeats of 10-fold cross validation, and sets of 10 sequences with mean accuracy 77.7% (Figure 7C upper panel).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on the DBN classification analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: When the DBN was asked to classify every sequence regardless of confidence level, the mean accuracy was 54.3%.
source: Where the DBN was asked to classify every sequence regardless of confidence level, the mean accuracy was 54.3%.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on the DBN classification analysis.

claim: When taking the 5% or 10% most confident assignments, individual sequences were classified with mean accuracy of 64.7% and 60.6% respectively.
source: When taking the 5% or 10% most confident assignments, individual sequences were classified with mean accuracy of 64.7% and 60.6% respectively, from 10-fold cross validation (Figure 7C lower panel).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section based on the DBN classification analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The response to sensitizer is accompanied by a dynamic, robust polyclonal increase in abundance of a defined set of TCR genes which presumably reflects clonal expansion of antigen-specific T cells in response to DPC.
source: The key findings are that the response to sensitizer is accompanied by a dynamic, robust polyclonal increase in abundance of a defined set of TCR genes which presumably reflects clonal expansion of antigen-specific T cells in response to DPC.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The breadth of the response to DPC, as captured by the number of TCRs that increase in frequency, is very diverse between individuals and predicts the degree of sensitization.
source: Notably, the breadth of the response, as captured by the number of TCRs that increase in frequency, is very diverse between individuals and predicts the degree of sensitization.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The response of individual TCRs to DPC is transient, with most TCRs returning to low frequencies, or disappearing by the subsequent time point.
source: Furthermore, the response of individual TCRs, which reflect individual T cell clonal dynamics, is transient, with most TCRs returning to low frequencies, or disappearing by the subsequent time point.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Activation of both CD4+ and CD8+ antigen-specific T cells plays key roles in allergic contact dermatitis.
source: There is widespread agreement that activation of both CD4+ and CD8+ antigen-specific T cells plays key roles, although antibody may also be important (Singleton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: The observed changes in TCR frequency from zero to eight are unlikely to be due to sampling effects.
source: The observed changes from zero to eight are unlikely to be due to sampling effects; in fact, modeling sampling as a Poisson process indicates that changes from zero to eight or more have individual probabilities of <0.05.
evidence: This is an argument stated in the Discussion based on statistical modeling.

claim: The observed TCR changes are unlikely to arise from exposure to unknown antigens (e.g. infectious agents).
source: The observed changes are also unlikely to arise from exposure to unknown antigens (e.g. infectious agents) since the number of expanded TCRs at the first time point post-sensitization is greater than the number of expanded TCRs observed in unsensitized individuals sampled at similar time points, for the great majority of the patients tested.
evidence: This is an argument stated in the Discussion based on comparison with control data.

claim: V and J gene skewing and increased CDR3 clustering are well-established signatures of an antigen-specific T cell response.
source: Moreover, the expanded set of TCRs show strong evidence of V and J gene skewing, and of increased CDR3 clustering, both well-established signatures of an antigen-specific T cell response (Thomas et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2017; Davis et al., 1995; Glanville et al., 2017; Dash et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The set of observations suggest that DPC stimulates a transient expansion of T cells carrying a defined set of related TCRs.
source: Taken together, this set of observations suggest that DPC, perhaps in the form of a set of modified-self peptide adjuncts, stimulates a transient expansion of T cells carrying a defined set of related TCRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: TCR clustering, V region enrichment, and DBN classification could be observed across a panel of unrelated individuals, suggesting that hapten-specific responses may be less dependent on MHC matching than conventional peptide-specific responses.
source: The observation that TCR clustering, V region enrichment, and DBN classification could be observed across a panel of unrelated individuals is particularly intriguing, and suggests that hapten-specific responses may be less dependent on MHC matching than conventional peptide-specific responses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the Discussion based on the observed patterns across individuals.

claim: DPC is considered a potent sensitizer.
source: DPC is considered a potent sensitizer (Stute et al., 1981; Mose et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The number of expanded TCRs at the first post-sensitization sample (2 weeks) showed strong correlation with the strength of the response.
source: This was reflected in a wide range of expanded TCRs, and the number of expanded TCRs at the first post-sensitization sample (2 weeks) showed strong correlation with the strength of the response.
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion.

claim: The reasons for inter-individual variation in response to DPC are unknown.
source: The reasons for this inter-individual variation are unknown, but could reflect inter-individual differences in immune response (Brodin et al., 2015), or potentially differences in factors that control hapten penetration, such as skin thickness or composition (Reynolds et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an acknowledgment of uncertainty with speculative explanations.

claim: Low responders to DPC were not boosted by repeated exposure over many months.
source: In our study, low responders were not boosted by repeated exposure to DPC over many months.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: The response to DPC was usually maximal at the first patch test, suggesting that regulatory mechanisms come into play to limit the response in vivo.
source: In fact, the response was usually maximal at the first patch test, suggesting that regulatory mechanisms come into play to limit the response in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion with an interpretive explanation.

claim: The initial TCR expansion did not continue to increase despite repeated exposure to antigen.
source: Similarly the initial TCR expansion did not continue to increase despite repeated exposure to antigen, and indeed the majority of TCRs showed very transitory responses, with individual TCR frequencies falling to around pre-sensitization frequencies by the next time point.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Similar rapid expansion and subsequent contraction of TCRs have been observed in response to live attenuated yellow fever vaccine.
source: Similar rapid expansion and subsequent contraction have been observed in response to live attenuated yellow fever vaccine (DeWitt et al., 2015; Pogorelyy et al., 2019; Pogorelyy et al., 2018), one of few examples where TCR repertoire has been studied before and after challenge in a human setting.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T cell contraction in the vaccine context may reflect the rapid disappearance of antigen.
source: T cell contraction in the vaccine context may therefore reflect the rapid disappearance of antigen.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation stated in the Discussion.

claim: The mechanisms which limit the DPC response are more likely to be due to intrinsic regulatory pathways or changes in intrinsic migratory pathways rather than simply reflect antigen disappearance.
source: The mechanisms which limit the DPC response are therefore more likely to be due to intrinsic regulatory pathways (e.g. Treg induction), or changes in intrinsic migratory pathways rather than simply reflect antigen disappearance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the Discussion based on the contrast with vaccine studies.

claim: A second wave of TCRs appeared at increased frequency at PT2, 6 weeks post-sensitization.
source: We noted that a second wave of TCRs appeared at increased frequency at PT2, 6 weeks post-sensitization.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: The set of 'late' TCRs at PT2 was almost completely distinct from the 'early' peak at week 2.
source: This set of 'late' TCRs was almost completely distinct from the 'early' peak at week 2.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: There was no correlation between the magnitude of the patch test score at PT1 and the number of TCRs expanded at PT2.
source: Furthermore, there was no correlation between the magnitude of the patch test score at PT1 and the number of TCRs expanded at PT2.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: This study is the first analysis of in vivo TCR repertoire changes in response to a chemical allergen.
source: In conclusion, this study is the first analysis of in vivo TCR repertoire changes in response to a chemical allergen, and is one of only a handful of studies that document in vivo longitudinal changes in TCRrep in response to immunization in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The immune response in this population may be different from healthy individuals, since all patients suffered from some form of alopecia, which is believed to have an autoimmune etiology.
source: We cannot rule out that the immune response in this population is different from healthy individuals, since all patients suffered from some form of alopecia, which is believed to have an autoimmune etiology (Trüeb and Dias, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the study.

claim: DPC is unlikely to bear any relation to the autoimmune target in alopecia, since similar therapeutic responses can be observed in patients with alopecia treated with other completely unrelated contact sensitizers.
source: Nevertheless, DPC is unlikely to bear any relation to the autoimmune target in alopecia, since similar therapeutic responses (hair growth) can be observed in patients with alopecia treated with other completely unrelated contact sensitizers.
evidence: This is an argument stated in the Discussion to address the potential limitation.

claim: The study confirms that the response even to a simple chemical such as DPC is polyclonal involving dozens or even hundreds of TCRs.
source: The study confirms our previous in vitro findings that the response even to a simple chemical such as DPC is polyclonal involving dozens or even hundreds of TCRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the study findings.

claim: The study highlights the dynamic nature of the TCR repertoire.
source: The study also highlights the dynamic nature of the TCR repertoire.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the study findings.

claim: A total of 34 patients were recruited to this study.
source: A total of 34 patients were recruited to this study (NRES Ethics Committee East of England – Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire [14/EE/1067]).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Participants were recruited from patients who had been diagnosed with alopecia and were identified as suitable for DPC treatment by a consultant dermatologist.
source: Participants were recruited from patients who had been diagnosed with alopecia, were aged between 18 and 70, identified as suitable for DPC treatment by a consultant dermatologist, and were now attending their first visit to the Alopecia Clinic at Salford Royal Hospital for DPC therapy.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: This study ran alongside patients' prescribed DPC treatment (weekly doses of DPC to the scalp to induce inflammation and hair regrowth).
source: This study ran alongside patients' prescribed DPC treatment (weekly doses of DPC to the scalp to induce inflammation and hair regrowth).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Twenty-nine of the individuals who participated in the study provided blood samples for TCR sequencing.
source: Twenty-nine of the individuals who participated in the study provided blood samples for TCR sequencing (TCRseq), for between one and four of the study time points (pre-sensitization, and at 2, 6, and 24 weeks of DPC treatment).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Flow cytometry data was obtained for peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 10 treated patients.
source: Flow cytometry data was obtained for peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 10 treated patients, and patch test data for 24 patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Patch test data was obtained for 24 patients.
source: Flow cytometry data was obtained for peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 10 treated patients, and patch test data for 24 patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Sensitization to DPC was induced by application of 2% DPC (in acetone) to a 2 cm by 2 cm patch of skin on the upper inner arm.
source: Sensitization to DPC was induced by application of 2% DPC (in acetone) to a 2 cm by 2 cm patch of skin on the upper inner arm.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Patch testing was performed on the skin of the upper back using Finn chambers (8 mm inner diameter) containing 0.01% DPC in acetone.
source: Patch testing was performed on the skin of the upper back using Finn chambers (8 mm inner diameter) containing 0.01% DPC in acetone.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: After 6 days, patients' reactions were scored according to standards set by the International Contact Dermatitis Research Group.
source: After 6 days, patients' reactions were scored as no reaction (−), weakly sensitized (+), strongly sensitized (++), or extremely sensitized (+++) according to standards set by the International Contact Dermatitis Research Group.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The α and β chains of the TCR repertoire were sequenced using a method that starts with total RNA isolated from unfractionated whole blood.
source: The α and β chains of the TCR repertoire of 29 participants were sequenced using a method that starts with total RNA isolated from unfractionated whole blood, collected in Tempus Blood RNA tubes (Thermofisher #4342792) using the manufacturer's protocol for RNA extraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The TCR sequencing pipeline introduces unique molecular identifiers attached to individual cDNA molecules to provide a quantitative and reproducible method of library preparation.
source: The pipeline introduces unique molecular identifiers attached to individual cDNA molecules to provide a quantitative and reproducible method of library preparation.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Naïve T cells were defined as CD45RA+ and CD27+.
source: Naïve cells were defined as CD45RA+ and CD27+; central memory as CD45RA− CD27+; effector memory as CD45RA− CD27−, and EMRA as CD45RA+ CD27−.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Central memory T cells were defined as CD45RA− CD27+.
source: Naïve cells were defined as CD45RA+ and CD27+; central memory as CD45RA− CD27+; effector memory as CD45RA− CD27−, and EMRA as CD45RA+ CD27−.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: EMRA T cells were defined as CD45RA+ CD27−.

claim: The pairwise similarity between TCRs was measured on the basis of amino acid triplet sharing using the normalized string kernel function.
source: The pairwise similarity between TCRs was measured on the basis of amino acid triplet sharing, which was calculated using the normalized string kernel function stringdot (with parameters stringdottype='spectrum', length = 3, normalized=TRUE) from the Kernlab package (Karatzoglou et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Two TCRs were considered connected if the similarity index was above 0.75.
source: Two TCRs were considered connected if the similarity index was above 0.75.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The DBN took as input the position along the CDR3 sequence, the amino acid in each position, the V and J genes, a position-specific triplet score, and a class score relative to sequence position.
source: The DBN took as input the position along the CDR3 sequence, the amino acid in each position, the V and J genes, a position-specific triplet score, and a class score relative to sequence position.

claim: The probability of observing a specific amino acid in a particular position given its neighbors differs between DPC-expanded sequences and control sequences.
source: For example, Figure 7B demonstrates the relationship between neighboring amino acids in specific positions in the CDR3 sequence and antigen specificity. The probability of observing a specific amino acid in a particular position given its neighbors differs between DPC-expanded sequences and control sequences.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7B.
